## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

# Game 5: Black vs 20k — W+12

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 39–40. There were 40 moves in total: 37 stone moves and three passes. The displayed next-move number was 41.
Final captures: Black 0, White 0. No ko or invalid move occurred.

20k was chosen deliberately after four losses, to practise living shapes and establish a baseline. This game also lost; no successful rank is established.

## Records and score
- game-005.sgf: complete 40-move record, including passes.
- game-005-log.json: opponent selection, every returned board, full move list, result, and final area inspection.
- Official result: White wins by 12 points.
- Manual final-board count, removing the dead Black D8/D9/E8/E9 stones: Black 38, White 43; White's 7 komi makes 50 against 38. There were no neutral points.
- Black's surviving lower group had 14 stones and 24 empty territory points. White had 19 stones and 24 territory points, including the four dead Black positions.

The tool displayed the dead Black stones on the final board; zero recorded captures does not mean they survived scoring. The independent area count agrees with the official margin.

## Main failure: too little area, followed by an invasion without a base
The first ten moves were:
1 B C3, 2 W G7, 3 B G3, 4 W C7, 5 B E5,
6 W C5, 7 B C4, 8 W G5, 9 B G4, 10 W E7.

Black obtained the lower side; White obtained the upper side. The area warning was recognized: even four complete rows are only 36 points, below Black's 45-point winning target with all points assigned. Nevertheless, subsequent play consolidated a lower region that ultimately scored only 38.

11 B D5, 12 W D6, 13 B D4 connected the left and central Black stones.
15 B B3 and 17 B A3 stopped White's left-side undercut.
19 B F5, 20 W F6, 21 B H5, 22 W G6,
23 B H4, 24 W H6, 25 B F4 connected the right side to the main Black chain.
27 B J4, 28 W J6 completed the edge boundary.

These moves produced a surviving lower group, but White's boundary remained farther down the board than Black needed. Securing a group was useful and insufficient for winning. At the final 38–43 split, shifting six points from White to Black would only draw (44–37 plus komi); seven would win (45–36 plus komi).

By move 28, E6 was surrounded by Black E5 and White D6/E7/F6. Black E6 would be suicide without a capture. The center had already closed; trying to repair the territorial deficit then required entering a much narrower upper region.

## Concrete failed invasion
29 B E8, 30 W F8,
31 B D8, 32 W C8,
33 B D9, 34 W C9,
35 B E9, 36 W F9.

E8 was played with a vague plan to spread along the top edge, rather than a demonstrated two-eye base or connection. White blocked both directions.

After White C8 at move 32, Black D8/E8 had D7/D9/E9 as liberties. D7 was already unusable: its other neighbors C7, D6 and E7 were White, and playing there would neither open a liberty nor capture a group. D9 and E9 were only two adjacent top-edge points, with White able to occupy the boundaries beyond them.

After move 36:
- Black D8/D9/E8/E9 had exactly one liberty: D7.
- White C7/C8/C9 still had B7, B8, B9, C6, D7.
- White D6 still had C6, D7, E6.
- White E7 still had D7, E6, F7.

Thus Black D7 was suicide: it would fill the Black group's last liberty and capture none of the three adjacent White groups. This was a dead four-stone block with zero eyes, not a ko or a nearly living top group.

D9/E9 enlarged the doomed group after its routes had narrowed. They did not establish eye space. The record does not prove E8 alone was objectively losing, but this continuation clearly failed. Do not reuse it as a working invasion pattern.

## What improved, and its limits
The lower Black group survived scoring. B3/A3 preserved the left boundary, H4 linked H5 to G4, F4 linked the right and central groups, and J4 preserved the edge boundary. A group/liberty inventory was run after every response from move 4 onward, including every contact decision; no own atari was overlooked.

However, the inventory exposed the top group's shrinking liberties without producing a strategic correction. At move 32 the only playable extensions led along a short first-line strip. Continuing to add stones repeated the previous games' mistake.

37 B pass, 38 W E6, 39 B pass, 40 W pass completed the game. Passing accepted a losing score; it was not a claim that Black had enough territory. Obtaining an actual score made the area deficit measurable.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k for another controlled experiment until basic living shapes and a scored win are repeatable. One loss does not establish an optimal rank; 9d remains the target.
2. Make the early count change the plan before the board closes. A lower framework of roughly 36–38 potential points needs a substantial additional region, not a one-point endgame repair.
3. Test an earlier contest of the center/upper boundary, for example reconsidering move 11 before D6/F6 arrive. E6 at that earlier stage is an unverified candidate, not an established best move. Do not infer that C3, G3 or E5 individually caused the loss.
4. Before entering behind a third-line boundary, name the two prospective eyes and the boundary moves that preserve them. An open first-line strip with enemy stones at both ends is not a base.
5. Count playable liberties separately from raw liberties when escape depends on one point. D7 was a liberty of the top group but Black could not legally occupy it.
6. Stop investing in a group when the proposed extension gains no viable eye or escape. After C8, D9/E9 added stones without solving life.
7. Preserve complete records and seek a numerical result when useful. Here 38–43 plus komi confirmed the earlier count and the deficit of the lower framework.

All decisions and review were manual. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move recommendation was used.

# Game 7: Black vs 20k — W+26

Final captures: Black 1, White 4. No ko or invalid move occurred.

- game-007.sgf contains all 62 moves.

- Official result: White wins by 26.

The diagonal opening was:
1 B C3, 2 W C7, 3 B G7, 4 W G3, 5 B E5,
6 W D5, 7 B E4, 8 W E3, 9 B D4, 10 W D6,
11 B E6, 12 W E2, 13 B E7, 14 W D8,
15 B C4, 16 W D7, 17 B E8, 18 W G6.

E6/E7 contested the upper boundary earlier than game 5, but this alone did not establish enough area. White obtained the upper-left and lower-right. White C2/C1/D2 also reduced the lower-left claim. Black B2/B1/B3/B4/A4 retained only a narrow left-side region.

During play, an unsupported rough estimate suggested about 45 potential points. A later explicit row count, before move 43, found only about 38 even if the top survived:
row 9 F–J: 4; rows 8–5 E–J: 20; row 4 A–E plus J4: 6;
row 3 A–D: 4; rows 2–1 A–B: 4. Total 38.
Several of these points were still unsecured. This was the same inadequate total as game 5, recognized after the boundary had largely closed.

The final Black region was that 38-point outline minus seven top points F8/G8/H8/F9/G9/H9/J9, yielding 31. This geometric comparison explains the final count; it is not a claim that all 38 were ever secure.

## Top fight: counter-atari did not guarantee a capture
40 W E9, 41 B F9, 42 W D9 left Black F9 disconnected with F8/G9 as its only liberties.
43 B G2 tenukied to an invasion.
44 W F8 put F9 in atari.
45 B G9, 46 W G8 left Black F9/G9 with only H9.
White F8/G8 had F7/H8 as liberties.

47 B F7 put White F8/G8 in atari at H8, but Black's own top chain was also in atari.
White could instead have played H9 immediately, capturing F9/G9 and opening F9/G9 as new liberties for F8/G8. Therefore F7 was not a forcing capture threat. This manually read variation was not played.

Actual continuation:
48 W H8, 49 B H9, 50 W H2,
51 B J8, 52 W J9 captured Black F9/G9/H9.
After that capture White F8/G8/H8 had F9/G9/H7/H9 as liberties.
53 B J7 saved the isolated J8 stone; 54 W F9 connected the invaders to the upper-left.
55 B H7 connected Black's main, right and edge stones; 56 W H9 connected White J9.

The mistake was already concrete at move 43: F9's vulnerable connection was left unresolved while starting another fight. F8 before tenuki is a manually suggested candidate that would connect F9 to E8 and prevent the actual F8 cut; it is not established as globally best or a winning correction. Do not reuse F9–G9–H9 as a safe first-line extension against this surrounding position.

Before a counter-atari, check whether the opponent can capture your group and thereby free theirs. This repeats game 1's capture-liberty lesson in a new shape.

## Lower invasion: abandoned after its base disappeared
43 B G2 entered the lower region without secured eye boundaries.
50 W H2 blocked the right extension.
58 W F2 left G2 with only G1.

A direct extension would not reach open space:
B G1, W F1 leaves Black G1/G2 only H1;
B H1 leaves the three-stone group only J1;
W J1 captures all three.
This is a manual variation, not an automated search or played continuation.

59 B D3 instead took the remaining main-group endgame point.
60 W G1 captured the single G2 stone. Black did not add further doomed extensions.
Calling F1/H1/J1 prospective eye points at invasion time was insufficient: Black had neither their boundaries nor the moves needed to secure them before White blocked.

## What survived, with an actual life proof
23 B F6 captured the invading White G6 stone. The capture reopened G6 for the neighboring Black stones.
37 B J4 was put in atari by 38 W J3; 39 B J5 connected it to H5 and saved it.
55 B H7 linked G7, H6 and J7, joining all remaining major Black stones.

After that connection:
- G6 was a true eye, bordered by connected Black F6/G5/G7/H6.
- J6 was a separate true eye, bordered by connected Black H6/J5/J7.
Thus the main group lived independently of the three-point A1/A2/A3 space.
A2 did not need to be filled to prove this group's life, because it already had the two independent right-side eyes.

57 B F5 and 59 B D3 claimed the remaining points along White's lower boundary.
61 B pass, 62 W pass ended the game. Passing accepted a losing score.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k. Three losses provide no basis to increase rank; aim for repeatable life and a scored win.
2. Make a row/region count by roughly moves 10–16 and revise it after invasions. A vague 45-point estimate must not overrule a concrete 38-point outline.
3. Repair vulnerable connections before tenuki. First-line F9 had no connection to E8 until F8 was secured.
4. A counter-atari can fail when the opponent captures first. Rebuild the board with every removed stone before counting the opponent's liberties.
5. Before invading, identify the boundary moves and their timing, not merely empty points where eyes might eventually appear. Do not repeat the G2 entry as a demonstrated living pattern.
6. Preserve a proven pair of eyes. G6/J6 show why naming connected boundaries is useful; the survival was real, but 31 area was far too small.

All moves and tactical variations were chosen/read manually. Code recorded responses, parsed current-board groups and liberties, converted moves to SGF and counted final present-board area. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or program selecting/ranking/recommending moves was used.

## Opening: three corner approaches were not three living groups
1 B E5, 2 W C7, 3 B G3, 4 W C3, 5 B C5,
6 W G7, 7 B G5, 8 W E7, 9 B E3,
10 W C6, 11 B H6, 12 W H7, 13 B J6,

Counting its potential correctly as unsecured was useful; failing to secure it still lost the game.

Earlier lower-left development, such as reconsidering B3 or C2 around move 10 instead of continuing the top, remains an unverified candidate. C2 alone is not a life pattern; game 6 already demonstrated that the left eye boundary and the dividing move also matter.

## Lower-left: two routes closed, then E4 added no liberties
22 W C4, 23 B B5, 24 W D4, 25 B B4,
26 W B3, 27 B D2, 28 W C2, 29 B D1,
30 W C1, 31 B A3.

White's seven-stone group then had only E4/B2/B1.
34 W E4, 35 B F4 left the eight-stone group only B2/B1.
E4 extended into a closed strip: it added F4 as a liberty, which Black immediately occupied. It neither escaped nor established an eye.

The corner extensions did not save this actual position:
- After move 35, W B2, B A2 leaves the enlarged White group only B1; W B1 leaves it only A1; B A1 captures it. Black's A2 connects to A3.
- Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves White only A1; W A1 is legal and extends to A2 as its sole liberty. B A2 then connects B2 to A3 and captures all ten White stones. A1 is not suicide in this variation: A2 is initially empty.

These are manual variations, not played moves or program search. They show why two remaining corner liberties were insufficient here.

Actual cleanup:
43 B A2, 45 B B1 put White in atari at B2;
47 B B2 captured all eight lower-left stones.
White did not add further doomed extensions.

The strategic correction belongs before A3/E2/F4 close the base and escape. No single earlier replacement has been verified to save the group or win.

## Right invasion: a narrow edge strip, not a base
36 W H3, 37 B H4, 38 W H2, 39 B G2,
40 W H1, 41 B G1.

After G1, White H3/H2/H1 had exactly J3/J2/J1 as liberties. All were in one straight edge strip. H4 and G3/G2/G1 barred the outside; J4 was not a secured White boundary. H1 preserved the corner approach but did not make two eyes.

53 B J3, 55 B J2 left the group only J1.
White J1 was suicide: Black J2/J3 retained J4 as a liberty.
57 B J1 captured all three White stones.

The invasion had no verified life plan when played. This repeats the earlier mistake of counting available edge points without their boundaries and timing. The lower region was already constrained; entering it late did not replace the lost corner.

## What survived: explicit eyes and successful invasion defense
42 W F7 joined F8, E7/F6 and G7/H7.
44 W B6 and 46 W A6 secured the left end of the wall.
48 W J7 closed the right edge; 49 B A5 fixed the left boundary.
50 W E8, 52 W D8, 54 W D9, 56 W F9 established:
- D7, bounded by connected White C7/D6/E7/D8.
- E9, bounded by connected White D9/E8/F9.
The main group had two independent true eyes before the later top invasions.

58 W pass, 59 B A7, 60 W B7, 61 B B8,
62 W C8, 63 B pass, 64 W C9, 65 B E1,
66 W A8 captured A7; 67 B C1;
68 W B9 captured B8.
C8/C9 secured the boundary before the captures. A8 retained A7/A9 immediately after capturing A7; no counter-capture freed the invaders. It later had A7/A9/B8, all bordered elsewhere by the living main group.

69 B H9, 70 W H8, 71 B pass,
72 W G9, 73 B J4, 74 W J9 captured H9.
The isolated J9 stone had H9/J8 afterward; both points were also adjacent to the living main group. Neither immediate Black entry could capture it. White's final A8 and J9 were separate stones supported by that living surrounding group, not standalone groups with two eyes.

75 B pass, 76 W pass finished the game.
The invasion defenses preserved 33 area; they did not repair the deficit.

3. Reassess the lower-left before the side undercut. C1 alone did not preserve the base; Black A3 invalidated its left eye boundary.
4. Identify the destination of an escape before extending. E4 added one temporary liberty F4, which Black filled immediately.
5. Three empty edge points need secured boundaries and a dividing move. H3/H2/H1 with only J1/J2/J3 was not alive.
6. The top defense worked because the main group already had D7/E9 and the invading stones' capture liberties were checked. Preserve this concrete reading, while separating life from a sufficient area count.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.

Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. 22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.

After Black A3, the lower-left had only E4/D3/B2/B1. C1 protected the right first-line boundary but did not preserve the left boundary. Black E2 connected E3 to D2/D1; White E4, Black F4 closed the last central route, leaving only B2/B1. Black A2/B1/B2 captured eight. Develop a second base before the wall and undercuts close it; no saving replacement is verified.

Alternatively W B1, B B2 leaves only A1; W A1 is legal but leaves only A2, where Black connects B2 to A3 and captures ten. Do not confuse this legal one-liberty extension with suicide.
